scenes.title: The Four Pillars of Futures Contracts

beatOutlines.textOutline: Card 1: Standardization - Exchange-traded agreements detailing quantity, quality, price, and date.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Card 2: Position Symmetry - Long agrees to buy the underlying; Short agrees to sell the underlying.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Card 3: Regulatory Boundaries - Daily price limits (limit up/down) and position limits on contracts.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Card 4: Convergence - Futures price converging to spot (F_T ≈ S_T) as delivery arrives.

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 1: Futures contracts are standardized, exchange-traded agreements to buy or sell an asset at a set price and date.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 2: Long positions commit to purchase the asset, while short positions commit to sell it.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 3: Payoff formulas scale price changes by contract size for both long and short positions.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 4: Standardized terms specify maturity windows, such as 15-25 years for T-bonds and 6.5-10 years for 10-Year T-notes.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 5: Quality adjustments enforce price parity, such as the 1.5 cent premium for No. 1 Yellow corn and 1.5 cent discount for No. 3.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 6: Exchanges enforce limit up/down bands and position limits to manage speculative volatility.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 7: Physical delivery occurs in under 1% of transactions, yet it serves as the essential pricing anchor.
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

beatOutlines.textOutline: Step 8: Impending delivery drives arbitrage, ensuring futures prices converge toward spot prices (F_T ≈ S_T).
beatOutlines.speaker: narrator

summarySteps: Futures contracts are exchange-traded, standardized commitments to buy or sell an asset at a predetermined date and price.
A long position commits to buying the underlying asset, whereas a short position commits to selling it.
Profits and losses scale through contract size: Exit - Entry for longs, and Entry - Exit for shorts.
Contract specs govern maturity and delivery assets, such as 15-25 year maturities for CME T-bonds versus 6.5-10 years for T-notes.
Commodity deliverable grades carry specific cash adjustments, like CME Corn's +1.5¢ premium for No. 1 Yellow and -1.5¢ discount for No. 3.
Exchanges limit volatility and exposure through daily price limits (limit up/down) and speculative position limits.
Although less than 1% of contracts settle physically, delivery obligations bind traders to exact operational requirements.
The potential for physical delivery enables arbitrage that forces futures prices to converge to spot prices (F_T ≈ S_T) at expiration.
bottomTakeaway: Standardization, exchange boundaries, and the physical delivery anchor work together to ensure orderly trading and complete price convergence between futures and spot markets.
